questions.stem: A deckhand is told to go into a ballast tank to inspect a weld. Under MOHS s. 169, what must exist before entry?
options: A work permit issued to the person entering
Nothing, provided the tank has been pumped empty
A verbal OK from the mate on watch
A life jacket worn over the coveralls
questions.explanation: Section 169 prohibits entering a confined space without a work permit issued under s. 166. An empty tank can still have a bad atmosphere.

questions.stem: Which of these jobs requires a written work permit under MOHS s. 166?
options: Work that requires entry into a confined space
Reading the draft marks from the dock
Coiling a mooring line on deck in port
Washing the wheelhouse windows from a ladder on deck
questions.explanation: Section 166(a) names confined space entry; paragraph (b) adds any work assessed as capable of causing death or serious injury, such as hot work.

questions.stem: Which set correctly describes a confined space under the MOHS definition?
options: Any compartment with a lockable door that is kept shut while the vessel is at sea
Any space smaller than 10 cubic metres, whatever its use, contents or ventilation
Enclosed, not meant for occupancy except for work, with restricted access and potentially hazardous
Any room below the waterline, including accommodation and the engine room
questions.explanation: The three tests are enclosure and no intended occupancy, restricted access and egress, and the potential to become hazardous. Size and location are not the test.

questions.stem: A marine chemist reads oxygen at 19.0 per cent in a void space. What is the correct decision?
options: No entry yet; 19.0 is below 19.5 per cent and must be corrected and held in range
Entry is fine, because 19 per cent is close enough to the normal 21
Entry is fine as long as the entrant wears a harness on a lifeline tended from outside
Entry is fine for up to five minutes with someone at the hatch
questions.explanation: Section 171(2)(c) requires 19.5 to 23 per cent by volume, with partial pressure of oxygen not below 148 mm Hg, and the value must be maintainable for the occupancy.

questions.stem: A reading of 24 per cent oxygen is found in a tank that has been ventilated with pure oxygen by mistake. What does the MOHS limit say?
options: It passes, because more oxygen makes the air safer to breathe in a tank
It passes if a fire watch with an extinguisher is posted at the hatch
It passes if the entrant is trained in confined space entry and carries a personal gas detector
It fails: it is above the 23 per cent limit, and oxygen must not be used for ventilation
questions.explanation: The upper limit is 23 per cent (MOHS s. 171(2)(c)); excess oxygen is a fire hazard. SWPR s. 35(a) bars the use of oxygen for ventilation.

questions.stem: Who carries out the atmosphere assessment before confined space entry under MOHS s. 171?
options: Any passenger who holds a current first aid certificate
A marine chemist or other qualified person the employer appoints
Any crew member who has worn a breathing apparatus
The deckhand who will enter, using a hand-held gas detector at the hatch
questions.explanation: The employer must appoint a marine chemist or other qualified person, who produces a signed written report.

questions.stem: How long is the confined space assessment report kept on the vessel (MOHS s. 172) and how long is a work permit kept (s. 168(2))?
options: The report for ten years and the permit for five years
Both for two years
The report for six months and the permit for one year
Both until the end of the voyage
questions.explanation: Section 172 requires the report to be kept on the vessel for two years from signing; s. 168(2) requires the permit to be kept for two years after the work is completed.

questions.stem: Which item is NOT among the things the employer must ensure before a confined space permit is issued under MOHS s. 173(1)?
options: That drowning liquid or entrapping solids are removed
That the space has been painted inside
That an entry control system is established
That inflow is prevented by disconnection or blank flanges
questions.explanation: Section 173(1) lists the written report, removal of liquids and solids, prevention of inflow, lockout, a big enough opening and an entry control system. Painting is not on the list.

questions.stem: Conditions in a tank cannot meet all the usual entry requirements. Which is part of the minimum under MOHS s. 173(3)?
options: A single deckhand who stands at the hatch with no means of calling for help
A life jacket and a hand-held torch for the person entering, and a radio
A harness on a lifeline anchored outside, held by a qualified attendant with an alarm
A sign reading Danger posted at the hatch, with the hatch left open
questions.explanation: Section 173(3) requires an attendant who is in communication and has an alarm, a harness on a lifeline anchored outside, two or more employees nearby, and one with first aid and emergency training.

questions.stem: Under SWPR s. 31, when may the person attending at the entrance of a ballast tank leave?
options: Only when the person inside has left, except in an emergency involving them
When the person inside reports by radio that all is well
Whenever they need a break, if another crew member is nearby
After ten minutes, if the atmosphere has been tested as safe
questions.explanation: Section 31(2) requires the attendant to remain until the person inside leaves, apart from an emergency with the person inside.

questions.stem: Before a hold or tank is closed off, who must make sure nobody is inside?
options: A qualified person (MOHS) or the person in charge of the work area (SWPR)
The next watch, when they take over the deck at change of shift
The harbour master or port authority, before the vessel sails
Nobody; the cover is just replaced once the work is done
questions.explanation: MOHS s. 173(4) requires a qualified person to verify; SWPR s. 32 puts the same duty on the person in charge of the working area.

questions.stem: Which definition fits hot work in MOHS s. 189?
options: Any work done in the engine room while the main engine runs
Any work in a hot space, such as close to the main engine exhaust manifold
Any work where flame is used or a source of ignition may be produced
Only welding or cutting with an oxy-acetylene torch on deck
questions.explanation: Section 189 is broad: flame or a possible source of ignition, so grinding sparks can count. Location and temperature are not the test.

questions.stem: Welding in a dry-dock void has just finished. The qualified person judges the area needs watching. For how long after the work may the fire watch continue?
options: 5 minutes
30 minutes
Until the next port
24 hours
questions.explanation: Section 190(a) requires a fire watch for the duration of the work and, if the qualified person thinks it necessary, for 30 minutes after. Section 190(b) adds enough extinguishers.

questions.stem: Hot work is planned in a compartment where flammable vapour may be present. What must happen first under MOHS s. 191(a)?
options: A warning sign is posted at the entrance and a fire extinguisher is placed close by the work
The workers put on respirators and a fire watch stands by while they proceed
It must be gas-freed, tested by a marine chemist or qualified person and found safe
A deckhand checks the air by smell before the torch is lit
questions.explanation: Section 191(a) requires gas-freeing, testing and a finding of safety by a marine chemist or other qualified person. Respirators do not remove an ignition risk.

questions.stem: Which gas must never be used to ventilate a compartment under SWPR s. 35?
options: Oxygen
Fresh air
Nitrogen only when told
Compressed air
questions.explanation: Section 35(a) says oxygen shall not be used for ventilation; it also bars use to blow out pipelines or clean (35(c) and (f)).
